title: “Monks, the perception of foulness, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as its end.…
content: “Monks, the perception of foulness, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as its end. For what reason is this said? When a monk dwells much with the perception of foulness, his mind retreats, turns back, and draws away from sexual intercourse, and thus his mind is not strained, becomes peaceful, and disenchantment arises. Just as, monks, a cock’s feather or a sinew thrown into fire retreats, turns back, draws away, and is not strained — so too, when a monk dwells much with the perception of foulness, his mind retreats, turns back, draws away from sexual intercourse, and thus his mind is not strained, becomes peaceful, and disenchantment arises. If a monk dwells much with the perception of foulness, yet his mind still runs after, gets stuck in sexual intercourse, and disenchantment does not arise, then he should understand: ‘The perception of foulness is not developed in me; there is no distinction before and after in me; I have not attained the fruit of development.’ There he is clearly aware. If a monk dwells much with the perception of foulness, his mind retreats, turns back, draws away from sexual intercourse, his mind is not strained, becomes peaceful, and disenchantment arises, then he should understand: ‘The perception of foulness is developed in me; there is a distinction before and after in me; I have attained the fruit of development.’ There he is clearly aware. That the perception of foulness, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as its end — for this reason it is said.”

title: “Dependent on attachment, this suffering arises. By the complete destruction of all attachments, suffering does not come to be. See the world with its multitude,…
content:
“Dependent on attachment, this suffering arises. By the complete destruction of all attachments, suffering does not come to be.

See the world with its multitude,
Overcome by ignorance,
Beings given to birth,
Delighting in becoming,
Not freed from existence.

For one who burns up existence,
At all times and places,
All this existence —
Impermanent, suffering, subject to change —

Seeing this as it really is
With perfect wisdom,
Craving for existence is abandoned,
As is the delight in non-existence.

With the complete destruction of craving,
Dispassion, cessation, complete,
That is Nibbāna.
That monk, cooled,
Without clinging to renewed existence,
Has conquered Māra,
Won the battle,
Crossed over all forms of existence.”

title: “Venerable sir, ‘stain’ is called a stain. What term is synonymous with what is called ‘stain’?” “Venerable sir, evil, unwholesome states, the realm of sensual…
content:
“Venerable sir, ‘stain’ is called a stain. What term is synonymous with what is called ‘stain’?”
“Venerable sir, evil, unwholesome states, the realm of sensual desire, are synonymous with what is called ‘stain.’”

title: “Here, Udāyi, a person lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments, the relinquishment of attachments. But while he lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments,…
content: “Here, Udāyi, a person lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments, the relinquishment of attachments. But while he lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments, the relinquishment of attachments, sometimes, from time to time, distorted thoughts, thoughts and considerations connected with attachments continue to arise. Udāyi, mindfulness arises slowly and he quickly abandons that thought, dispels it, ends it, destroys it. Udāyi, just as a man might drop two or three drops of water onto an iron pan that has been heated all day—slowly those drops fall, quickly they evaporate and vanish. Udāyi, I say: ‘This person is still bound, not freed.’ Why is that? Udāyi, the difference in his faculties has been fully understood by me.”

title: “And, lord of gods, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does…
content: “And, lord of gods, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in those forms, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then, because he does not delight, does not praise, and dwells without lust, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Without clinging, lord of gods, that monk attains Nibbāna. There are sounds cognizable by the ear … odors … tastes … touches … Lord of gods, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in those phenomena, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then, because he does not delight, does not praise, and dwells without lust, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Without clinging, lord of gods, that monk attains Nibbāna. This, lord of gods, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here and now attain Nibbāna.”

title: “And how, friend, does one guard the sense faculties? Here, friend, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp the…
content: “And how, friend, does one guard the sense faculties? Here, friend, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — he restrains that cause, guards the eye, practices restraint of the eye. When he hears a sound with the ear … smells an odor with the nose … tastes a flavor with the tongue … feels a touch with the body … cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — he restrains that cause, guards the mind, practices restraint of the mind. Thus, friend, is the guarding of the sense faculties.”

title: Where the mind is restrained, There suffering ends. If the mind is fully restrained, One is fully freed from suffering. (The Blessed One): One should…
content:
Where the mind is restrained,
There suffering ends.
If the mind is fully restrained,
One is fully freed from suffering.

(The Blessed One):
One should not restrain the mind
Completely in every way.
Do not restrain the mind
When self-control is attained.
Where evil states arise,
There one should restrain the mind.

title: “Monks, suppose the Ganges river carries along a great pile of foam. A person with good eyesight would look at it, reflect, and examine it.…
content: “Monks, suppose the Ganges river carries along a great pile of foam. A person with good eyesight would look at it, reflect, and examine it. Looking, reflecting, examining, the foam would appear empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a pile of foam? So too, monks, whatever form there is, past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near — a monk sees form, reflects, examines it. Seeing, reflecting, examining, form appears empty, hollow, insubstantial. For what substance could there be in form?”

title: “Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple reflects: ‘Now I am being overwhelmed by form. In the past, I was also overwhelmed by form just as…
content: “Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple reflects: ‘Now I am being overwhelmed by form. In the past, I was also overwhelmed by form just as I am now being overwhelmed by present form. If I were to delight in future form, then in the future I would be overwhelmed by form just as I am now being overwhelmed by present form.’ Reflecting thus, he has no regret for past form, no delight in future form, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.”

title: “That is so, great king. Few are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, do not become infatuated, do not become intoxicated,…
content:
“That is so, great king. Few are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, do not become infatuated, do not become intoxicated, do not fall into heedlessness regarding sensual pleasures, and do not act wrongly toward others. But many are those in the world who, having obtained abundant, great wealth, become infatuated, intoxicated, fall into heedlessness regarding sensual pleasures, and act wrongly toward others.

Bemused by wealth and sensual pleasures,
People are greedy and deluded,
In the midst of sensual pleasures,
Without clear awareness,
They are overly intoxicated,
Like a deer unaware of the trap set —
Later they suffer,
Experiencing the results of evil deeds.”
